description: We are just here for the gist of it
summary:
ARES·LUNA is an interactive planetary analog intelligence and mission-planning platform for NASA’s Permanent Moon Base and Mars challenge. It helps users explore lunar and Martian candidate environments, compare them with Earth analog locations, and understand which places could support testing rovers, habitats, spacesuits, scientific instruments, and exploration systems.

The platform combines a 3D Moon/Mars explorer, Earth analog discovery, exact-site imagery and maps, scientific comparison dashboards, mission resource simulation, ranking tools, educational explanations, and NASA/ESA/CSA/JAXA source references. It uses NASA-linked resources such as LRO Diviner, LRO LOLA, NASA PDS, MRO datasets, EMIT, SRTM, HLS, RADARSAT, Copernicus, ESA Open Science Catalog, and JAXA G-Portal.

ARES·LUNA makes complex planetary science easier to understand while clearly separating verified source context from illustrative prototype assumptions. This gives students, educators, engineers, and mission planners a transparent way to explore where Earth-based testing could prepare humanity for long-duration lunar and Martian missions.
details:
ARES·LUNA is a web-based planetary analog intelligence and mission simulation platform created for NASA’s Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars challenge. It helps users explore Moon and Mars candidate locations, discover comparable Earth environments, compare terrain and environmental characteristics, and simulate mission requirements.

The platform includes an educational landing experience, interactive Moon/Mars exploration, Earth analog discovery, 3D visualization, exact-site maps and imagery, candidate ranking, scientific comparison panels, mission planning, and AI-assisted explanations. It uses NASA and partner-agency resources including LRO, MRO, NASA PDS, EMIT, SRTM, HLS, RADARSAT, Copernicus, ESA Open Science Catalog, and JAXA G-Portal as source references.

The frontend was built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, and Lucide icons. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, and scikit-learn. The application is deployed with Vercel for the frontend and Railway for the backend.

The project’s intended impact is to make planetary science and mission planning more understandable, transparent, and engaging for students, educators, engineers, and the public. Some engineering values and scores are clearly labeled as illustrative prototype estimates rather than direct satellite measurements.
